Numerical simulation of these governing equations provides the means to quantitatively describe the concentration profiles across the GB region, which are then used to obtain GB solute drag P expressed in non-dimensional P¯ form as31

P¯ = \frac{Pv a}{kB T} = - \sum i=B,C \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (ci - c\infty i) \frac{dE¯ i}{dx¯} dx¯, (8)

where va is the atomic volume. In this work, all computational studies are reported using the non-dimensional parameters discussed above. These model parameters can be mapped onto real metallic alloy values as follows: A representative GB width in a typical metallic alloy is 2\delta = 1 nm and thermal energy kB T \approx 0.08 eV assuming an annealing temperature in the range 800-1000 K, typical in metallic alloys59. At such temperatures, experimentally measured GB velocities are in the range Vref \approx 0.1-10 \mu m s-1 60 and representative values for GB solute diffusion \approx 10-15 m2 s-1 45,61.

The foregoing exposition underscores several key advantages of the proposed model. First, the model requires as input physical parameters that can be directly obtained from atomistic simulations. For example, atomistic methods have been employed to calculate GB diffusivity45, bulk Onsager transport coefficients46, GB chemical free energies via thermodynamic integration62, and bulk heat of mixing derived from alloy phase diagrams63–65. Second, our model enables the direct simulation of coupled diffusive processes governing GB solute drag, thereby establishing a quantitative link between atomic-scale mechanisms and experimentally observed GB phenomena. Here, we note that the GB geometry is described by five macroscopic degrees of freedom66, three for misorientation and two for plane normal, and that each GB geometry has its unique thermodynamic and kinetic properties. We also note that establishing GB structure-property linkages relating the GB’s thermodynamic and transport properties to its geometric degrees of freedom is one of the most active areas of research in GB physics. While this work does not consider anisotropic boundary segregation, it is straightforward to include anisotropy effects in our modeling treatment by allowing the model parameters describing the GB segregation energy and diffusion coefficients to be functions of the boundary geometry. In addition to the dependence of GB segregation on boundary geometry9,10,67, several studies revealed site-specific GB segregation, in which the segregation energy depends on the local atomic environment within the GB68–70. This results in distributions for the GB segregation energy in terms of the atomic environment, even for the same GB geometry43,71,72. Accounting for site-specific segregation for a given GB can be achieved in our treatment by allowing our model parameters to be distributions rather than single-valued quantities.

Model Assumptions

Our proposed modeling treatment considers multi-element segregation and migration of planar GBs using a one-dimensional bicrystal geometry. As a result, the relevant transport coefficients are solute diffusion across the GB. A future extension of our model to 2D/3D geometries would enable the incorporation of a tensorial description of GB diffusion in which both diffusion along and across the GB are incorporated. Indeed, atomistic simulations of Cu-Ag binary alloys, for example, showed that accelerated lateral GB diffusion leads to non uniform redistribution of solute atoms, which in turn influences GB solute drag73. Such a 2D/3D extension of our model will capture the dynamics of GB networks, thereby allowing us to investigate the interplay between GB segregation and phenomena such as abnormal grain growth. Our model treats GBs as regions with thermodynamic properties that are distinct from the bulk, resulting in a segregation energy that is single-valued. It is interesting to extend our treatment to account for site-specific GB segregation, in which the segregation energy is given by a distribution due to the local atomic environment of the GB. This can be incorporated into our treatment by allowing the model parameters that describe the GB segregation energy to be distributions rather than single-valued quantities. Our work considers solid solution alloys in order to deconvolute solute drag effects due to multi-element GB segregation from GB pinning due to second-phase precipitates. It would be interesting to investigate in future work the interplay between GB segregation and phase separation and their net impact on GB migration kinetics. Finally, another extension of our modeling framework is to explicitly consider vacancies and their interactions with GBs, as several studies revealed vacancy generation and emission at migrating boundaries51,52. This can be achieved by treating GBs as sources/sinks of such points defects with prescribed interaction energies.

Multicomponent Segregation Isotherm

We begin our exploration of the model by investigating the equilibrium GB concentrations of stationary boundaries, i.e., V=0. In this case, the GB solute concentration is obtained using the parallel tangent construction74, in which parallel tangents to the bulk and GB free energy surfaces are drawn at the equilibrium bulk c\infty i and GB cgb i concentrations of the ith solute, see Fig. 1(b). This construction results in an analytical solution for the concentration ci(x) of solute i at a distance x from the center of the GB, which is given by

ci(x) = c\infty i + (cgb i - c\infty i) exp [ -E¯ i(x) + 2\Omega¯b Ai (ci(x) - c\infty i) - \Omega¯b(cj(x) - c\infty j) ], i,j=B,C, j \neq i, (9)

Equation 9 defines a multicomponent segregation isotherm describing the GB concentrations as a function of far-field bulk concentrations c\infty i = c(x \to \infty), i = B,C and the alloy model parameters. The segregation isotherm given by Eq. 9 can be mapped onto the treatment by Guttmann75 who investigated equilibrium GB segregation in ternary alloys. However, we note here that Guttmann’s model75 only considered solute-solute interactions in the GB layer as it assumed the bulk phase to be an ideal, dilute alloy. Therefore, our segregation isotherm given by Eq. 9 extends Guttmann’s treatment by introducing both bulk and GB solute-solute interactions. It is interesting to note from Eqs. 4 and 9 that the expressions for the GB solute concentrations are coupled through the solute interaction parameters, where the GB concentration of one solute type depends on the boundary concentration of the other solute types. To demonstrate this multicomponent coupling effect, we consider two ternary alloy classes. The first is an alloy, I where both solutes B and C segregate to the GB. For the second alloy, solute B is chosen to segregate to the GB, while solute C desegregates. Capturing such contrasting segregation behaviors in our model can be achieved in many ways. One possible scenario is through the bulk solute interaction parameter \Omega¯b AC and the results are shown in Fig. 2. For the alloy where both solutes segregate to the GB, we set \Omega¯b AC = 1.5, while for the second alloy, where solute B segregates and solute C desegregates, we let \Omega¯b AC = -1.5. All other models parameters for both alloys are set the same and are shown in Fig. 2(a) and (e), where we assume ideal GBs, i.e., boundary interaction parameters \Omega¯gb AC = \Omega¯gb BC = \Omega¯gb AB = 0.

Panels (a) through (d) of Fig. 2 depict results for the alloy, where both solutes segregate to the GB, while panels (e) through (h) of Fig. 2 show results for the alloy with B(C) segregation(desegregation).

Surface plots of the boundary concentrations at the center of the GB where \Upsilon = 1, cgb B and cgb C, as a function of the bulk alloy concentrations c\infty B and c\infty C are respectively shown in Fig. 2(b) and (f) for the alloy where both solutes segregate to the GB and the second alloy with B(C) segregation(desegregation). These surface plots show that GB concentrations are sensitively dependent on bulk alloy concentrations c\infty B and c\infty C. To highlight such dependencies, we use these surface plots to construct GB concentration line scans as a function of bulk concentrations, and the results are shown in Fig. 2(c), (d), (g), and (h), where the dashed line in black is the unity line. For the alloy where both solutes segregate to the GB, Fig. 2(c) shows a plot of the GB concentration cgb B as a function of c\infty B for various values of c\infty C and Fig. 2(d) shows one of the GB concentration cgb C as a function of c\infty C for various values of c\infty B. For this alloy, it can be seen that the GB solute concentrations cgb B and cgb C increase with the bulk concentrations.

Furthermore, it can be clearly seen that cgb B depends sensitively on the concentration of the second solute c\infty C and a similar trend holds for cgb C, see Fig. 2(d). For the second alloy case, where solute B segregates to the GB and solute C desegregates, Fig. 2(g) shows a plot of the GB concentration cgb B as a function of c\infty B for various values of c\infty C and Fig. 2(h) shows one of the GB concentration cgb C as a function of c\infty C for various values of c\infty B. For this alloy, it can be seen that increasing the bulk concentration c\infty B leads to an increase in GB solute concentration cgb B, and that such an increase is less sensitive to the bulk concentration of C, c\infty C. Also shown in Fig. 2(h) is a plot of GB concentration cgb C as a function of bulk concentration c\infty C, where the GB concentration falls below the bulk values (i.e., below the unity line) indicating desegregation of solute C at the GB. For this alloy with B(C) segregation(desegregation), \Delta G¯ AB = \Delta G¯ AC = 0.5 and the bulk solute interaction parameter between A and C is \Omega¯b AC = -1.5. This indicates a stronger attractive A-C interactions in the bulk compared to the driving force for segregation of C described by \Delta G¯ AC, noting that we set the GB interaction parameters \Omega¯gb AC = \Omega¯gb BC = \Omega¯gb AB = 0. The interested reader is referred to Supplementary_Code.zip for a Python script to plot the multicomponent GB segregation isotherms as a function of the model parameters.

Dynamics of Doped Grain Boundaries

We now direct our attention to GB dynamics and the impact of GB diffusion coefficients on solute drag-velocity profiles. To this end, we employ the two alloy cases discussed in Fig. 2, namely a ternary alloy with \Omega¯b AC = 1.5 resulting in both solutes B and C segregating to the GB, and a second alloy with \Omega¯b AC = -1.5 leading to the segregation of solute B and desegregation of solute C. All other model parameters for both alloys are the same and shown in Fig. 2(a) and (e). In this analysis, we set the cross-diffusion coefficients D¯gb BC = D¯gb CB = 0 and perform simulations varying D¯gb BB and D¯gb CC, which describe the diffusion of solutes B and C, respectively. Figure 3 shows results demonstrating the impact of D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC on GB concentrations and solute drag-velocity profiles. Figure 3(a)–(c) depicts results for the ternary alloy case, where both solutes B and C segregate to the GB, and Fig. 3(d)–(f) shows results for the alloy with B(C) segregation(desegregation).

For the ternary alloy, where both solutes B and C segregate to the GB, Fig. 3(a) shows concentration profiles across the GB region at a boundary velocity V¯ = 1 for various values of D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC. It can be seen that the GB concentration of solute B increases with D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC and that when D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC = 1 the concentrations of both solutes have the same profile. Here, we note that in this alloy case both solutes have the same segregation energy, i.e., \Delta G¯ AB = \Delta G¯ AC = 0.5 and \Omega¯b AB = \Omega¯b AC = 1.5. The corresponding solute drag-velocity profiles for the cases with D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC = 0.1, 1, and 10 are shown in Fig. 3(b). It can be seen that having a fast diffusing segregating solute results in drag-velocity profiles that maintain large values of solute drag beyond the peak point, i.e., a more gradual drop in solute drag past the max solute drag point. For this alloy, the thermodynamic parameters describing GB segregation are symmetric with respect to the exchange of B and C (i.e., \Delta G¯ AB = \Delta G¯ AC and \Omega¯b AB = \Omega¯b AC). However, having different values for D¯gb BB and D¯gb CC breaks this segregation symmetry and leads to concentration profiles of B and C that are different. For this ternary alloy system, where both solutes B and C segregate to the GB, the drag P¯* and GB velocity V¯* values at the peak point of the solute drag-velocity profiles are obtained as a function of D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC and plotted in Fig. 3(c). The peak points in solute drag-velocity profiles shift to larger drag and velocity values with increasing D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC until D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC = 1, which corresponds to alloys where both solutes have the same segregation energies and diffusivities. Then, a gradual decrease in P¯* and V¯* is observed in cases with D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC > 1. While the alloy system depicted in Fig. 3(a)–(c) considers cases where both solutes have the same segregation energy, Fig. 3(c) clearly shows that solute drag effects in multicomponent alloys are sensitively dependant on the operative mass transport processes.

Results for the ternary alloy where solute B segregates to the GB and solute C desegregates are shown in Fig. 3(d)–(f). As discussed above, desegregation of solute C in this ternary alloy case is driven by attractive bulk A-C interactions set by \Omega¯b AC = -1.5. Solute concentration profiles using a GB velocity V¯ = 1 for various values of D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC are shown in Fig. 3(d), where it can be seen that increasing D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC leads to an increase in the GB concentration of solute B and a concomitant decrease in the boundary concentration of solute C. This can be explained as follows: according to Eq. 4, the segregation energy of solute i depends on the heat of mixing parameters of various solute types which are coupled through the concentration fields. For this alloy case, the segregation energy of solute C, Ei (see Eq. 4), depends on the concentration of B through the term \Omega¯b AC cB with \Omega¯b AC = -1.5. As a result, increasing the GB concentration of B reduces the segregation energy of solute C, a trend observed in Fig. 3(d).

Next, Fig. 3(e) shows the corresponding solute drag-velocity profiles for various values of D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC, where it can be seen that the location of the peak point in drag-velocity profiles shifts to larger velocity values with increasing D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC. Using these drag-velocity profiles, the drag P¯* and GB velocity V¯* values at the peak points are plotted in Fig. 3(f) as a function of D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC. A monotonic behavior of P¯* and V¯* is observed, in which P¯* decreases and V¯* shifts to larger values with increasing D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC. This trend for the ternary alloy with B(C) segregation(desegregation) is in contrast to the alloy case where both solutes segregate to the GB, Fig. 3(a), which depicts a non-monotonic behavior for P¯* and V¯* as a function of D¯gb BB/D¯gb CC. The results depicted in Fig. 3 demonstrate the complex GB chemical states and resultant solute drag-velocity profiles that arise due to multicomponent coupling effects. It is interesting to note that while many published studies76,77 suggest GB solute segregation as a strategy to control GB migration, Fig. 3 reveals that in multicomponent systems GB desegregation of a solute type can be as effective in inducing GB solute drag and, therefore, controlling boundary dynamics. For example, comparison of Fig. 3(c) and (f) shows that choosing alloys, where one solute type segregates to the GB and a second that desegregates results in boundary drag values that are comparable in magnitude to alloys where both solutes segregate to the GB. Furthermore, the results depicted in Fig. 3 demonstrate that a quantitative understanding of the impact of GB chemistry on boundary migration in multicomponent alloys requires in addition to the segregation energies of solutes a detailed knowledge of mass transport processes in such alloys.

In Fig. 3, we explored the impact of GB mass transport processes on boundary solute drag using ternary alloys with contrasting segregation behaviors, namely an alloy system where both solutes segregate to the GB and a second alloy with B(C) segregation(desegregation). We now consider the impact of far-field bulk concentration level of both solutes (i.e., c\infty B and c\infty C) on solute drag values. Classical models predict that GB solute drag in binary alloys increases linearly with bulk concentration31. This linear scaling is a direct manifestation of the ideal and dilute solution thermodynamics assumption employed in these modeling treatments. Such assumptions, however, are not valid in multicomponent alloys, especially ones with far-from-dilute concentrations.

To demonstrate the impact of bulk concentration on solute drag, we employ the same ternary alloy classes considered in Figs. 2 and 3, specifically ones with various values for the bulk heat of mixing parameter \Omega¯b AC. We consider cases with \Omega¯b AC = -1.5, 0, and 1.5, while keeping the other alloy model parameters the same, shown in Fig. 4(a), and use D¯gb BB = D¯gb CC = 1.0 and D¯gb BC = D¯gb CB = 0.0. Then, we perform simulations with various bulk concentration values and obtain resultant solute drag-velocity profiles. Figure 4(b) shows contour slices depicting the peak solute drag P¯* as a function of the interaction parameter \Omega¯b AC and bulk concentrations c\infty B and c\infty C. These contour slices reveal several trends. First, the maximum solute drag exhibit a non-monotonic dependence on bulk concentrations c\infty B and c\infty C. For example, the ternary alloy with \Omega¯b AC = 1.5 shows that P¯* increases with c\infty B and c\infty C over some range of concentrations then decreases with increasing bulk concentrations. Second, the ternary alloy with \Omega¯b AC = -1.5, resulting in the segregation of solute B to the GB and desegregation of solute C, yields large solute drag values compared to the ideal alloy case with \Omega¯b AC = 0. Third, for the model parameters used in Fig. 4(a) regimes in bulk concentration space with large solute drag values do not align with lines of equi-concentration of solutes.

In metal physics, multicomponent alloys with equi-atomic concentrations, i.e., so-called high entropy alloys, have been the subject of active research as they exhibit unique engineering and functional properties78,79. Considering ternary alloys with equiatomic solute concentrations, as indicated by the dashed lines in Fig. 4(b), Fig. 4(c) presents the peak solute drag P¯* plotted along the c\infty B = c\infty C concentration line. It can be seen that for the ternary alloys with various values of \Omega¯b AC considered here, the peak solute drag value increases with concentration along this equi-concentration line until it reaches a maximum then it decreases with increasing the bulk concentration. The trends observed in Fig. 4 can be understood by examining Eq. 4, which reveals using the model parameters in Fig. 4(a) that the segregation energies of B and C at the center of the GB are given by EB = -2 + 3cB + (1.5 + \Omega¯b AC)cC and EC = -0.5 + (2cB - 1)\Omega¯b AC + (1.5 + \Omega¯b AC)cB demonstrating that the GB segregation energy of solute i is coupled to the concentration of solute j through the heat of mixing model parameter \Omega¯b AC. This is in contrast to existing studies of solute drag in multicomponent alloys38–40, which assume ideal and dilute alloys, resulting in concentration-independent and decoupled segregation energies for the various species. A key outcome of these assumptions is that GB solute drag scales linearly with bulk composition. The results depicted in Fig. 4 clearly demonstrate that GB solute drag exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on bulk compositions and that such dependence is sensitive to the nature of solute interactions.

To further illustrate the complex GB concentration profiles arising due to multicomponent alloying effects and its impact on boundary solute drag, we now consider the inverse problem. Specifically, we explore the so-called one-to-many relationships in which alloy systems with various thermodynamic properties and GB segregation characteristics result in the same solute drag profiles. As a demonstration, we select three ternary alloys, termed Alloy 1, Alloy 2, and Alloy 3, with contrasting segregation behaviors, yet resulting in near identical GB solute drag-velocity profiles. This is achieved in our model through the three bulk heat of mixing parameters, namely \Omega¯b AB, \Omega¯b AC, and \Omega¯b BC, while fixing all other model parameters, including the dilute-limit segregation energy \Delta G¯ AB = \Delta G¯ AC = 0.1, and the results are shown in Fig. 5. Figure 5(a) shows values of the bulk heat of mixing parameters, \Omega¯b AB, \Omega¯b AC, and \Omega¯b BC, used for these alloys, while Fig. 5(b) shows the rest of the model parameters used in these systems.

We set bulk concentrations c\infty B = c\infty C = 0.1 and let D¯gb BB = D¯gb CC = 1.0 and D¯gb BC = D¯gb CB = 0.0. For Alloy 1, the bulk regular solution parameters for A-B and A-C pairs are \Omega¯b AB = \Omega¯b AC = 1.5, which results in both solutes B and C having the same segregation energy. For Alloy 2, we set \Omega¯b AB = \Omega¯b BC = 0 and \Omega¯b AC = 1.5, which models zero bulk interaction energy for A-B and B-C pairs and repulsive interactions in the bulk for A-C. According to Eq. 4, the additional component to GB segregation energy due to repulsive bulk A-C interactions leads to a competitive segregation effect in which the stronger segregation of solute C result in an induced desegregation of B. For Alloy 3, the bulk regular solution parameters for the A-B, A-C, and B-C are \Omega¯b AB = \Omega¯b AC = \Omega¯b BC = -1.5 favoring bulk alloy mixing which result in desegregation of solutes B and C from the GB.

At a GB velocity V¯ = 1, Fig. 5(c) shows the concentration profiles of solutes B and C across the GB for all three alloys, Alloy 1, Alloy 2, and Alloy 3. As expected, GB segregation of both solutes B and C is observed in Alloy 1, where segregation of solute C and desegregation of solute B is seen in Alloy 2. For Alloy 3, desegregation of both solutes B and C can be observed. Figure 5(d) shows the corresponding GB solute drag-velocity profiles for these three alloy systems, which reveal near identical solute drag profiles, specifically the peak solute drag value and the corresponding velocity at the peak solute drag point. The results depicted in Fig. 5 clearly demonstrate multicomponent effects, in which alloys with contrasting segregation behaviors and GB concentrations can result in identical boundary drag profiles. While studies77,80 proposed GB solute segregation as a strategy to control GB dynamics in binary alloys, Fig. 5(c) and (d) reveals a broader alloy design space in multicomponent systems, where solute desegregation, for example, can be as effective in controlling GB dynamics. Indeed, experimental studies on multicomponent alloys revealed GB segregation of some solute types and desegregation of other alloying element types18,81.

The results depicted in Figs. 2 through 5 explore alloys with various bulk heat of mixing parameters, while assuming ideal GBs with no interactions between elements A, B, and C within the boundary region, i.e., \Omega¯gb AC = \Omega¯gb AB = \Omega¯gb BC = 0. We now direct our attention to the impact of GB heat of mixing on solute drag. To this end, we explore alloys with various values for the GB heat of mixing \Omega¯gb BC while fixing all other model parameters, shown in Fig. 6(a). Again, in regular solution thermodynamics \Omega¯gb BC describes the interaction energy of alloying elements B and C within the GB region, where negative (positive) values for \Omega¯gb BC describe attractive (repulsive) B-C interactions. Here, we let \Delta G¯ AB = 0.1 and \Delta G¯ AC = 0.05 indicating slightly stronger GB segregation of solute B than that of C, recall from Eq. 4 that \Delta G¯ AB and \Delta G¯ AC represent segregation energies in the dilute limit. Also, we set \Omega¯gb AC = \Omega¯gb AB = 0 indicating no A-C and A-B interactions within the GB in order to isolate effects due to B-C interactions described by \Omega¯gb BC. We employ alloys with a bulk concentration of c\infty B = c\infty C = 0.1 and set the diffusion coefficients to D¯gb BB = D¯gb CC = 1.0, D¯gb BC = D¯gb CB = 0.0. Using Eq. 9 for the multicomponent segregation isotherms at zero velocity, Fig. 6(b) shows equilibrium concentrations at the center of the boundary region as a function of the GB heat of mixing \Omega¯gb BC, where it can be seen that GB concentrations of solutes B and C decrease with the increase in \Omega¯gb BC. For the alloy model parameters employed in Fig. 6, the GB concentration of solute C decreases below the bulk level for some range of \Omega¯gb BC values indicating GB desegregation of C. In such a case, the higher GB concentration of solute B due to its larger segregation energy than that of C combined with repulsive B-C interactions set using large values of \Omega¯gb BC result in an induced desegregation case where segregation of B drives desegregation of C. At a GB velocity V¯ = 1, Fig. 6(c) shows concentration profiles across the GB region for various values of \Omega¯gb BC. Decreasing \Omega¯gb BC to negative values, indicating attractive B-C interactions within the boundary, leads to synergistic co-segregation of both solutes. Furthermore, Fig. 6(c) reveals an induced desegregation case for large values of \Omega¯gb BC (i.e., repulsive B-C interactions at the GB), in which segregation of solute B drives desegregation of C. The corresponding GB solute drag-velocity profiles for the ternary alloy systems with various values of \Omega¯gb BC are shown in Fig. 6(d). The markers in magenta identify peak GB solute drag values, which are shown in the inset of Fig. 6(d) as a function of \Omega¯gb BC. It can be clearly seen that GB solute drag is sensitively dependent on solute-solute interactions within the GB region, where an increase in \Omega¯gb BC results in a reduction in the solute content at the GB, see Fig. 6(c), and a decrease in solute drag values. On the other hand, negative values of \Omega¯gb BC indicate attractive GB B-C interactions resulting in synergistic co-segregation of both solutes and an increase in GB solute drag.

All results presented so far do not consider the impact of off-diagonal diffusion coefficients D¯gb BC and D¯gb CB on solute drag, which we investigate now.

To this end, we employ the alloy with the model parameters depicted in Fig. 6(a) and use \Omega¯gb BC = 1.5, i.e., repulsive B-C interactions within the GB. We set D¯gb BB = D¯gb CC = 1.0 and perform simulations systematically varying the off-diagonal diffusion coefficients D¯gb BC and D¯gb CB. Recall that the diffusion coefficients can be expressed as Dij = \sum k Lik \partial\mu k / \partial cj, where Lik are the Onsager coefficients and \partial\mu k / \partial cj are the thermodynamic factors, and that the values and algebraic sign of the off-diagonal diffusion coefficients are influenced by both Lik and \partial\mu k / \partial cj. For example, a negative value for D¯gb BC indicates diffusion of solute B up the concentration gradient of solute C. Figure 7 shows results demonstrating the role of off-diagonal diffusion coefficients in GB solute drag, where the contour plots in Fig. 7(a) and (b) show respectively the dependence of the peak solute drag P¯* and velocity V¯* at peak point on D¯gb BC and D¯gb CB. It can be seen that solute drag is sensitively dependent on the magnitude and algebraic sign of the off-diagonal diffusion coefficients. For the model parameters chosen here which favor the segregation of solute B over C, there exists a combination of D¯gb BC and D¯gb CB values that maximizes GB solute drag. In general, D¯gb BC and D¯gb CB do not have the same values, and Fig. 7(a) shows that solute drag P¯* decreases in regimes where D¯gb BC and D¯gb CB are dissimilar. Figure 7(b) reveals a general trend where the velocity V¯* at peak drag decreases with the increase in both D¯gb BC and D¯gb CB. A close examination of panels (a) and (b) of Fig. 7 reveals that V¯* is much more sensitive to variations in D¯gb BC and D¯gb CB than the peak solute drag P¯*. To demonstrate how the concentration profiles are influenced by the off-diagonal diffusion coefficients D¯gb BC and D¯gb CB, Fig. 7(c) shows GB concentration line scans for solutes B and C in two cases, namely one with D¯gb BC = D¯gb CB = 0 and a second with D¯gb BC = -1 and D¯gb CB = 1.

According to Eqs. 5 and 7, the use of non-zero values for D¯gb BC and D¯gb CB results in coupling of the governing equations for solutes B and C, where the evolution of one solute type is also driven by the chemical potential gradients of the other solute types. This is seen in Fig. 7(c) where the GB concentration profiles are sensitive to the particular values of D¯gb BC and D¯gb CB. Using D¯gb BC = -1 for this alloy with \Omega¯gb BC = 1.5 leads to diffusion of B up the concentration gradient of C while also maintaining repulsive B-C interactions within the GB region.

Figures 3 and 7 show that in addition to the segregation energy of each alloying element, a detailed knowledge of the operative transport processes is equally important as mass transport in multicomponent alloys is characterized by several diffusion coefficients with potentially large contrast in their magnitudes46. For example, even in ternary alloys with equal segregation energies for solutes B and C, our simulation results, see Fig. 7, reveal that varying the diffusion coefficients results in drastic changes to GB solute drag-velocity profiles.

Model Parametrization and Validation

The proposed modeling framework, together with the simulations it produces, provides several pathways for cross-validation with established databases, experimental observations, and atomistic simulations. First, our modeling treatment explicitly accounts for both bulk and GB free energies, parametrized using regular solution thermodynamics. The bulk regular solution model parameters can be obtained from existing thermodynamic databases85. For example, for the PtAuPd50, FeNiZr82, and CuAlY84 ternary alloys, in which experimental observations revealed GB segregation, Table 1 lists reported values for the bulk regular solution model parameters of the constituent binary pairs50,86. On the other hand, GB-solute interactions for each solute type can be computed using atomistic simulations68,87. For example, for the Cu-Ag alloy atomistic simulations employing thermodynamic integration in conjunction with the Gibbs adsorption equation were used to calculate the GB free energy as a function of Ag concentration62. These atomistically-obtained GB free energies can then be fit to regular solution free energy expressions to obtain the GB heat of mixing model parameters. Several studies reported values for GB regular solution model parameters in various alloys, such as \Omega¯gb AlMg = -4.6 in Al-Mg at 327°C88,89 and \Omega¯gb NiP = 6.2 in Fe-Ni-P at 475°C90.

A second avenue for validating our modeling results is comparison with experimental GB segregation data. Here, it is important to note that direct, in situ characterization of concurrent GB migration, solute segregation, and solute drag is constrained by limited spatial and temporal resolution and by the difficulty of isolating individual boundaries in polycrystalline metallic alloys. Nevertheless, recent advances in microscopy have enabled detailed quantification of chemical profiles across static GBs, providing a direct means to validate predictions from our model. To demonstrate this cross-validation strategy, we consider the PtAuPd ternary alloy in which recent experiments revealed GB segregation50. We simulate GB segregation in Pt0.76Au0.18Pd0.06 (in at.%) using reported bulk heat of mixing model parameters50 shown in Table 1 while assuming ideal GBs, and the results are shown in Fig. 8. Our modeling results depicting concentration profiles across a stationary GB are shown in Fig. 8(a), where segregation of Au is observed accompanied by depletion of Pt while the Pd concentration profile does not show any significant enrichment at the GB. Xing et al.50 experimentally investigated GB segregation in the PtAuPd alloy with various compositions and temperatures. For a Pt0.76Au0.18Pd0.06 alloy annealed at 800°C for 24 hrs, Fig. 8(b) shows chemical line scans across a GB using energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) revealing Au segregation to the Pt GB with no tendency for Pd segregation. Figure 8 reveals that our modeling results [Fig. 8(a)] are in qualitative agreement with experimental EDS line scans [Fig. 8(b)] in terms of segregation profiles. This approach of comparing GB concentration line scans from our model with those obtained experimentally provides avenues to validate our simulation results.

In summary, we presented a theoretical and computational model of GB segregation and solute drag in multicomponent alloys that accounts for both GB and bulk solute-solute interactions of various alloying elements. Ternary alloys were employed as they represent a model system with multicomponent effects while offering computational tractability. Analytical analysis recovered a multicomponent segregation isotherm, describing the GB solute content as a function of the thermodynamic properties the alloy. Simulation results revealed that solute interactions of various elemental pairs resulting in segregation behaviors, such as synergistic co-segregation and induced desegregation, greatly influence the characteristics of GB solute drag-velocity profiles. In addition to the segregation energy of solutes, our work highlights the need to account for the transport coefficients of various alloying elements in order to have a quantitative understanding of GB solute drag in multicomponent systems. Computational studies demonstrated that GB solute drag can exhibit a non-monotonic dependence on bulk concentrations, in contrast to existing solute drag models which only consider binary alloys. Furthermore, it was shown that in multicomponent alloys GB desegregation can be as effective in inducing GB solute drag, thereby expanding the alloy design space in applications where controlling GB dynamical processes is a key microstructural goal. While GB segregation has been extensively studied, prior work has largely been confined to the chemistry of static boundaries. Predictions from our modeling framework motivate future research by shifting the focus to GB dynamics, coupled evolution of boundary segregation and solute drag, as a strategy for designing advanced alloys with tailored microstructures.

### Reviewer 1

The paper presents a computational study of solute segregation at grain boundaries and solute drag in disordered ternary
alloys. The simulations utilize the phase-field approach based on regular solution thermodynamics. This is a classical
metallurgical subject that has been studied for many years. However, most of the previous work has been done on binary
systems. To my knowledge, this is the first systematic computational study of solute drag in a ternary system. The parametric
exploration reveals several important trends related to solute co-segregation and solute competition. The results also
demonstrate the sensitive dependence of the solute drag force on the solute interaction parameters and the relative diffusion
coefficients of the three components. This work provides a glimpse into the complexity of grain boundary dynamics in
multicomponent systems, including high-entropy alloys.
The paper makes a significant contribution to the field of grain boundary-solute interactions in multicomponent systems and
presents the results very clearly. As such, I recommend the paper for publication after the authors address the following
suggestions.
1. Many readers will try to translate the computational results to real-world alloys. Although the simulations were carried out
using dimensionless variables, it would help if the authors discussed some typical values of the physical parameters
corresponding to simulation conditions. For example, the dimensionless grain boundary velocity varies between 0 and 15.
What are the corresponding physical velocities in meters per second? Similar estimates could be made for the solute
interaction parameters and the diffusion coefficients.
2. The regular solution model predicts a miscibility gap and a critical point of mixing. Such gaps are different in grain
boundaries and inside the grains. The simulations utilized interaction parameters that kept both solutions above the
respective critical points. The authors could mention that, under real conditions, the segregation atmosphere could undergo
a phase separation, which would drastically change the solute drag dynamics. The impact of grain boundary phase
separation was studied in binary systems (e.g., https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2019.08.046) but might be studied in ternary
systems by changing the interaction parameters within the present model.
3. The model studied here is essentially one-dimensional. As a result, solute diffusion along the grain boundary is not
considered. Meanwhile, lateral diffusion plays a significant role in the solute drag (https://doi.org/10.3390/nano11092348).
The authors may want to mention this fact as one of the limitations of the model, which could be addressed if the authors
decide to extend their model to 2D in the future.
Yuri Mishin.

### Reviewer 2

The authors present a model for grain boundary segregation and solute drag in multicomponent alloys, incorporating solute-
solute interactions. While the manuscript is well-written and presents some interesting results, I do not believe it passes the
bar for publication in Nature Communications.
1) My biggest criticism is the failure to acknowledge prior literature. Equation (9), presented as a novel multicomponent
segregation isotherm, is, in fact, the classical Guttmann isotherm [Guttmann, Surface Science 53.1 (1975)], which the
authors should be familiar with. This oversight significantly undermines the perceived novelty of the work.
2) On the same note, the statement that "There are no GB solute drag models that consider multicomponent alloying effects"
is inaccurate. Models addressing this exist, such as those by Bréchet and Purdy [Acta materialia 51.18 (2003)], Mendelev
and Srolovitz [Interface Science 10 (2002)], and Hersent et al. [DOI: 10.4236/mnsms.2014.41002]. For example, the work by
Bréchet and Purdy extended the classic Cahn’s treatment to multicomponent systems, and explored the impact of solute-
solute interactions on drag in ternary systems. While these models may have limitations (e.g., dilute concentration
assumptions), a rigorous comparison is essential. The manuscript would benefit significantly from a thorough review of these
models, clearly articulating the advantages of the proposed approach, such as its ability to capture non-dilute behavior, and
critically evaluating the limitations of prior work, including what physics, if any, were missed.
3) Although I think the current model represents an improvement over the prior models, it still retains a main limiting
assumption of the prior models, specifically the assumption of a single average segregation energy (single site type) at the
grain boundaries. This simplification fails to account for: (a) grain boundary segregation anisotropy, a crucial factor in solute
drag, as demonstrated by prior work from the corresponding author [Barr et al., Nanoscale 13.6 (2021)]. And, (b) the site-
dependent nature of segregation, which leads to diverse co-segregation behaviors that cannot be captured by the averaged
approach. see [Scheiber et al., Scripta materialia 150 (2018)] and [Wagih et al., arXiv:2411.05303].
4) Can the current model capture experimentally observed abnormal grain growth?
5) The provided code only solves for the equilibrium segregation isotherm (which is not the main contribution of the paper).
The authors should also include the code used to solve the dynamic solute drag equations, which would be more beneficial
to the community.
Given that this work extends the authors' previous model [Physical Review Letters 127.17 (2021)] to multicomponent alloys,
and primarily focuses on a parametric study, it appears more appropriate, after revision, for a specialized journal in
computational materials science.

### Reviewer 3

The authors have employed theoretical models and computational methods to study the grain boundary (GB) segregation
behaviors, and the associated GB solute drag in multicomponent alloys. Their model accounts for thermodynamic solute
interactions between different alloying elements in both the bulk and GB regions, as well as the multicomponent diffusion of
these alloying elements. Furthermore, the GB solute drag is quantified through the solute concentration profiles near the GB
under a constant migration velocity. This study systematically examines the effects of GB diffusion coefficients, bulk solute
concentration, bulk solute interactions, and GB solute interactions on the GB solute drag-velocity relationship, contributing to
a deeper understanding of GB solute drag in multicomponent alloys.
This work addresses an important topic in alloy design by providing valuable insights into GB solute drag in multicomponent
alloy systems. The study is well-motivated, and the theoretical approach is appropriate for the investigation. However,
several scientific concerns need to be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication. My detailed
comments are as follows:
Comments:
1) Regarding solute segregation thermodynamics, the expressions for free energy and chemical potential in the ternary alloy
system, based on the regular solution model, appear to be a straightforward extension of those for a binary alloy system,
as described in the authors’ earlier works 1,2. The primary novelty of the current study seems to lie in the investigation of GB
solute drag in multicomponent alloys. Nevertheless, as noted in Comment 2, the effect of multicomponent diffusion on GB
solute drag remains insufficiently understood in the present work.
2) In the context of multicomponent diffusion, especially in far-from-dilute alloys, the kinetic coupling between different solute
fluxes is crucial, as it significantly influences the solute concentration distribution near the GB and, consequently, the GB
solute drag. However, the manuscript neglects the cross-diffusion process between solute B and C within the GB by
assuming D_BC^gb=D_CB^gb=0 in all calculations, meaning that the off-diagonal kinetic transport coefficients in the
Onsager matrix are set to zero. This assumption of ignoring kinetic coupling between solute fluxes must be justified, and its
impact on the results should be clarified.
3) Related to comment 2, the off-diagonal transport coefficients are closely associated with solute-solute interactions and
solute concentrations. Specifically, positive or negative solute-solute interactions can normally lead to distinct solute
diffusion behaviors, thereby affecting the GB solute drag effect. Therefore, solute cross-diffusion coefficients and solute-
solute interactions should not be considered independent.
4) What is the temperature value used in the calculations? Generally, an increase in temperature enhances solute diffusion
while reducing solute segregation tendencies and solute interactions. The authors should clarify the role of temperature in
their model and discuss its effect on GB solute drag in multicomponent alloys.
5) It is widely reported that GB migration is associated with vacancy generation and emission, mediated by vacancy diffusion
near the GB. How does the vacancy concentration distribution affect solute diffusion in multicomponent alloys and,
consequently, the GB solute drag? The authors should clarify whether vacancy effects are considered in their model and
mention their potential impact on the results.
6) Regarding the results in Figure 5, the authors state that solute B preferentially desegregates from the GB in Alloy 2.
Nevertheless, the values of Ω_AB^b=0 and ΔG_AB=0.1 shown in Figure 5(a) suggest a tendency for solute B to segregate
at the GB, which appears inconsistent with the stated conclusion.
